notes.front: What is a Falco condition?
notes.back: The key part of a Falco rule: a Boolean predicate over event fields that decides whether an event matches the rule.
notes.explanation: Conditions are written in Falco's condition syntax and can test any supported event through its supported fields.
notes.example: Like a search filter in an email client (from = boss and subject contains urgent), but applied to system events such as a process starting in a container.
notes.evidence: The key part of a rule is the condition field. A condition is a Boolean predicate expressed using the condition syntax.
notes.source: Falco docs, Basic Elements of Falco Rules, “Conditions”

notes.front: What is a Falco output?
notes.back: The message a rule emits when it matches: a string that can include event fields written with a % prefix, filled in like printf.
notes.explanation: An output can use the same fields that conditions use, so the alert shows the values from the event that matched.
notes.example: Like a mail-merge letter with blanks for name and address, but the blanks are %user.name and %container.id.
notes.evidence: A rule output is a string that can use the same fields that conditions can use prepended by % to perform interpolation, akin to printf.
notes.source: Falco docs, Basic Elements of Falco Rules, “Output”

notes.front: What is a Falco macro?
notes.back: A named, reusable piece of condition that rules (and other macros) can include instead of repeating it.
notes.explanation: Falco's docs describe macros as a way to define common sub-portions of rules in a reusable way.
notes.example: Like a named cell range in a spreadsheet that many formulas refer to, but holding a piece of condition such as “the event is in a container”.
notes.evidence: Macros provide a way to define common sub-portions of rules in a reusable way.
notes.source: Falco docs, Basic Elements of Falco Rules, “Macros”

notes.front: What is a Falco list?
notes.back: A named collection of items, such as process names, that rules, macros or other lists can include.
notes.explanation: Referring to a list inserts its items where it is used, so one list can be shared by many rules.
notes.example: Like a contacts group in an address book: name it once, then use the group wherever you would type each address.
notes.evidence: Lists are named collections of items that you can include in rules, macros, or even other lists.
notes.source: Falco docs, Basic Elements of Falco Rules, “Lists”

notes.front: What is falco_rules.local.yaml?
notes.back: The rules file, in /etc/falco, for your own custom rules; the default configuration loads it after the default falco_rules.yaml.
notes.explanation: The default falco.yaml loads falco_rules.yaml, then the custom rules in falco_rules.local.yaml, then the rules.d directory.
notes.example: Like a house-rules sheet pinned under the landlord's standard tenancy terms: read after them, and able to add to them.
notes.evidence: makes Falco load rules from the /etc/falco/falco_rules.yaml file, followed by any custom rules located in the /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml file
notes.source: Falco docs, Default and Local Rules Files, “The configuration file”

notes.front: Which required Falco rule key holds a short, unique name for the rule?
notes.back: rule
notes.explanation: The rule key is one of five required keys; the other four are condition, desc, output and priority.
notes.evidence: rule yes A short, unique name for the rule.
notes.source: Falco docs, Basic Elements of Falco Rules, “Advanced Rule Syntax”

notes.front: Which required Falco rule key holds a longer description of what the rule detects?
notes.back: desc
notes.explanation: desc is required, like rule, condition, output and priority.
notes.evidence: desc yes A longer description of what the rule detects.
notes.source: Falco docs, Basic Elements of Falco Rules, “Advanced Rule Syntax”

notes.front: Which required Falco rule key holds the filtering expression applied to events?
notes.back: condition
notes.explanation: Events that satisfy this expression match the rule.
notes.evidence: condition yes A filtering expression that is applied against events to check whether they match the rule.
notes.source: Falco docs, Basic Elements of Falco Rules, “Advanced Rule Syntax”

notes.front: Which required Falco rule key specifies the message sent when a matching event occurs?
notes.back: output
notes.explanation: Without an output a rule is incomplete, since output is one of the five required keys.
notes.evidence: output yes Specifies the message that should be output if a matching event occurs.
notes.source: Falco docs, Basic Elements of Falco Rules, “Advanced Rule Syntax”

notes.front: Which required Falco rule key gives the severity of the event, and is it case-sensitive?
notes.back: priority; it is case-insensitive (emergency, alert, critical, error, warning, notice, informational or debug).
notes.explanation: The docs describe it as a case-insensitive representation of the event's severity.
notes.evidence: priority yes A case-insensitive representation of the severity of the event.
notes.source: Falco docs, Basic Elements of Falco Rules, “Advanced Rule Syntax”

notes.front: What happens to a Falco rule with enabled: false?
notes.back: It is neither loaded nor matched against any events. The default is true.
notes.explanation: enabled is an optional key, so leaving it out keeps the rule active.
notes.evidence: If set to false, a rule is neither loaded nor matched against any events.
notes.source: Falco docs, Basic Elements of Falco Rules, “Advanced Rule Syntax”

notes.front: Which optional Falco rule key holds cases that stop the rule from generating an alert?
notes.back: exceptions
notes.explanation: exceptions is optional, like enabled and tags.
notes.evidence: exceptions no A set of exceptions that cause the rule to not generate an alert.
notes.source: Falco docs, Basic Elements of Falco Rules, “Advanced Rule Syntax”

notes.front: A custom Falco rule has rule, condition, output and priority keys, but Falco rejects it as incomplete. Which required key is missing?
notes.back: desc
notes.explanation: rule, condition, desc, output and priority are the five required keys; the others are optional.
notes.evidence: desc yes A longer description of what the rule detects.

choicesExplained.enabled: enabled is optional and defaults to true.

notes.source: Falco docs, Basic Elements of Falco Rules, “Advanced Rule Syntax”

notes.front: The condition container.id != host and proc.name = bash has no system-call clause. What happens when bash starts in a container?
notes.back: Falco outputs an event for every syscall that shell performs, because the condition only checks event metadata.
notes.explanation: With no event type in the condition, every syscall from that bash process matches.
notes.evidence: Since this condition does not include a clause with a system call it will only check event metadata. Because of that, if a bash shell does start up in a container, Falco outputs events for every syscall that is performed by that shell.
notes.source: Falco docs, Basic Elements of Falco Rules, “Conditions”

notes.front: In a Falco condition, what does the clause container.id != host check?
notes.back: That the event happened inside a container rather than on the host.
notes.explanation: For a process on the host, container.id is the string host, so any other value means a container.
notes.evidence: The first clause checks that the event happened in a container (where container.id is not equal to "host" as the event occurs in a container).
notes.source: Falco docs, Basic Elements of Falco Rules, “Conditions”

notes.front: To alert only when a bash shell is spawned in a container, not on its every syscall, use: {{c1::(evt.type in (execve, execveat))}} and container.id != host and proc.name = bash
notes.back: (evt.type in (execve, execveat))
notes.explanation: Adding the event types for starting a program limits the rule to each successful spawn of the shell.
notes.evidence: If you want to be alerted only for each successful spawn of a shell in a container, add the appropriate event types to the condition: (evt.type in (execve, execveat)) and container.id != host and proc.name = bash
notes.source: Falco docs, Basic Elements of Falco Rules, “Conditions”

notes.front: You must alert once each time sh or bash is started inside any container, and never for shells on the node itself. Which condition fits?
choices: evt.type in (execve, execveat) and container.id != host and proc.name in (sh, bash)
container.id != host and proc.name in (sh, bash)
evt.type in (execve, execveat) and container.id = host and proc.name in (sh, bash)
evt.type in (execve, execveat) and proc.name in (sh, bash)
notes.back: evt.type in (execve, execveat) and container.id != host and proc.name in (sh, bash)
notes.explanation: It needs all three parts: the spawn event types, the in-a-container test, and the process names.
notes.evidence: (evt.type in (execve, execveat)) and container.id != host and proc.name = bash

choicesExplained.container.id != host and proc.name in (s: With no event type it matches every syscall of the shell, not once per start.

Without the container clause it also alerts for shells on the node.

notes.back: spawned_process and container and shell_procs
notes.explanation: The docs build the same shell_in_container rule from these macros, joined with and.
notes.evidence: spawned_process and container and shell_procs

choicesExplained.spawned_process or container or shell_pr: With or, any process spawn anywhere would match.

notes.front: A Falco output includes %container.image.repository, but the event happened on the host. What is printed for that field?
notes.back: `<NA>` (not available), because the field is not set for that event.
notes.explanation: Not every field has to be set in every event; for an unset field Falco prints this marker instead of a value.
notes.evidence: if the connection happens outside a container the field %container.image.repository would not be set and <NA> is displayed instead.
notes.source: Falco docs, Basic Elements of Falco Rules, “Output”

notes.front: Can a Falco output use transform operators such as toupper(), as conditions can?
notes.back: Yes, e.g. user=%toupper(user.name).
notes.explanation: The docs show %toupper(user.name) turning root into ROOT in the alert.
notes.evidence: Outputs can also use the transform operators that are used in conditions.
notes.source: Falco docs, Basic Elements of Falco Rules, “Output”

notes.front: An incident team wants each Falco alert to show the Kubernetes Pod name and namespace. Which output fragment does that?
notes.back: pod=%k8s.pod.name ns=%k8s.ns.name
notes.explanation: Output fields are interpolated only when prefixed with %, and k8s.pod.name and k8s.ns.name hold the Pod name and namespace.
notes.evidence: A rule output is a string that can use the same fields that conditions can use prepended by % to perform interpolation, akin to printf.

choicesExplained.pod=k8s.pod.name ns=k8s.ns.name: Without %, the field names are printed as plain text.

notes.front: Does a Falco rule's priority decide which rule is triggered first, or let it override another rule?
notes.back: No. Priority is only severity; trigger order is controlled by the order in which rules are defined and loaded.
notes.explanation: The docs warn: “Don't let the priority field name mislead you.”
notes.evidence: In a Falco Rule, it has nothing to do with overriding another rule or choosing the order in which rules will be triggered. The way to control the latter is achieved by changing the order the rules are defined and therefore loaded.
notes.source: Falco docs, Basic Elements of Falco Rules, “Priority”

choices: Only the severity shown in its alerts
It now runs before all other rules
It now overrides the default rule with the same condition
It is now loaded first from falco_rules.yaml
notes.back: Only the severity shown in its alerts.
notes.explanation: Priority indicates how serious a violation is and appears in the output; order is set by where rules are defined and loaded.
notes.evidence: Every Falco rule has a priority which indicates how serious a violation of the rule is.

choicesExplained.It now runs before all other rules: Trigger order comes from the order rules are defined and loaded, not priority.
choicesExplained.It now overrides the default rule with t: Priority has nothing to do with overriding another rule.
Which file a rule is in, and the rules_files order, decide loading.

notes.source: Falco docs, Basic Elements of Falco Rules, “Priority”

notes.front: What conditions do Falco's default macros container and spawned_process stand for?
notes.back: container: container.id != host. spawned_process: evt.type in (execve, execveat).
notes.explanation: The docs define both as macros because many rules would repeat them, and note both are in the default list.

notes.front: Can a Falco macro refer to another macro that is defined later in the rules files? Can it refer to a list defined later?
notes.back: Another macro: no, it must be defined before. A list: yes, a macro can reference any list.
notes.explanation: Visibility cascades: lists and macros must see same-kind objects defined earlier, but a macro can use any list and a rule any macro.

notes.source: Falco docs, Basic Elements of Falco Rules, “Visibility”

Define a list with that condition and use it in each rule
Put the clause in each rule's output
notes.back: Define a macro with that condition and use its name in each rule.

notes.evidence: Macros provide a way to define common sub-portions of rules in a reusable way.

notes.source: Falco docs, Supported Fields for Conditions and Outputs, “Field Class: container (plugin)”

notes.front: How do the Falco fields proc.name and proc.cmdline differ?
notes.back: proc.name is the process name (truncated after 16 characters); proc.cmdline is the name plus its arguments.
notes.explanation: proc.cmdline concatenates proc.name and proc.args, truncated after 4096 bytes.
notes.evidence: The concatenation of proc.name + proc.args (truncated after 4096 bytes) when starting the process generating the event.
notes.source: Falco docs, Supported Fields for Conditions and Outputs, “Field Class: process”

notes.front: What does NIST SP 800-190 say container-aware runtime tools should build, and use for what?
notes.back: Security profiles of containerised apps, learned from behaviour, used to prevent and detect anomalies at runtime.
notes.explanation: NIST says existing host-based intrusion detection is often unable to detect attacks within containers.
notes.evidence: These tools should be able to automatically profile containerized apps using behavioral learning and build security profiles for them to minimize human interaction. These profiles should then be able to prevent and detect anomalies at runtime
notes.source: NIST SP 800-190, §4.4.4 App vulnerabilities, p. 25

notes.front: An nginx container that only ever runs nginx suddenly starts /usr/bin/python3. Which NIST SP 800-190 runtime anomaly is this?
choices: Changes to protected configuration files and binaries
Traffic sent to unexpected network destinations
notes.back: Invalid or unexpected process execution
notes.explanation: A program the app never runs is an unexpected process, the first anomaly NIST lists.
notes.evidence: Invalid or unexpected process execution,

choicesExplained.Creation of unexpected network listeners: Nothing here opens a listening port.
choicesExplained.Changes to protected configuration files: No file is changed; a program is run.

notes.source: NIST SP 800-190, §4.4.4 App vulnerabilities, p. 25

notes.front: A web app's container, which has never done so, starts making ptrace and mount system calls. Which NIST SP 800-190 runtime anomaly is this?
choices: Writes to unexpected locations and file types
notes.back: Invalid or unexpected system calls
notes.explanation: NIST lists unexpected system calls as its own class of runtime anomaly, separate from process execution.
notes.evidence: Invalid or unexpected system calls,

choicesExplained.Malware storage or execution: Nothing identifies malware; the anomaly is the calls themselves.

notes.source: NIST SP 800-190, §4.4.4 App vulnerabilities, p. 25

notes.front: Inside a running container, /etc/passwd and /bin/ls are modified. Which NIST SP 800-190 runtime anomaly is this?
choices: Changes to protected configuration files and binaries
Traffic sent to unexpected network destinations
notes.back: Changes to protected configuration files and binaries
notes.explanation: A system configuration file and a binary have been changed, which NIST names directly.
notes.evidence: Changes to protected configuration files and binaries,

choicesExplained.Invalid or unexpected process execution: The event is a change to files, not a program being run.
choicesExplained.Invalid or unexpected system calls: NIST lists changes to protected files as their own anomaly.

notes.source: NIST SP 800-190, §4.4.4 App vulnerabilities, p. 25

notes.front: A container that only writes logs to /var/log/app starts creating .so library files under /dev/shm. Which NIST SP 800-190 runtime anomaly is this?
choices: Writes to unexpected locations and file types
Changes to protected configuration files and binaries
notes.back: Writes to unexpected locations and file types
notes.explanation: Both the place and the kind of file are outside what the app normally writes.
notes.evidence: Writes to unexpected locations and file types,

choicesExplained.Changes to protected configuration files: New files are created; no existing protected file is changed.
choicesExplained.Invalid or unexpected process execution: Nothing says a new program was run.

notes.source: NIST SP 800-190, §4.4.4 App vulnerabilities, p. 25

notes.front: A batch-job container that never serves traffic begins listening on port 4444. Which NIST SP 800-190 runtime anomaly is this?
choices: Traffic sent to unexpected network destinations
notes.back: Creation of unexpected network listeners
notes.explanation: Opening a port to accept connections is a new listener; NIST treats outbound traffic separately.
notes.evidence: Creation of unexpected network listeners,

choicesExplained.Traffic sent to unexpected network desti: That covers traffic going out, not a port waiting for connections.
choicesExplained.Invalid or unexpected system calls: NIST names new listeners as their own anomaly.

notes.source: NIST SP 800-190, §4.4.4 App vulnerabilities, p. 25

notes.front: A payments container that only talks to its database starts sending data to an unknown address abroad. Which NIST SP 800-190 runtime anomaly is this?
choices: Traffic sent to unexpected network destinations
Writes to unexpected locations and file types
Changes to protected configuration files and binaries
notes.back: Traffic sent to unexpected network destinations
notes.explanation: The destination is outside what the app normally contacts.
notes.evidence: Traffic sent to unexpected network destinations, and

choicesExplained.Creation of unexpected network listeners: The container is sending, not listening.

notes.source: NIST SP 800-190, §4.4.4 App vulnerabilities, p. 25

notes.front: NIST SP 800-190's list of runtime anomalies ends with traffic sent to unexpected network destinations, and {{c1::malware storage or execution}}.
notes.back: malware storage or execution
notes.explanation: It completes NIST's seven examples of events that runtime security profiles should detect.
notes.evidence: Traffic sent to unexpected network destinations, and Malware storage or execution.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-190, §4.4.4 App vulnerabilities, p. 25

notes.front: What does readOnlyRootFilesystem: true in a container's securityContext do?
notes.back: Mounts the container's root filesystem as read-only.
notes.explanation: It is one of the container-level security context settings in the Kubernetes task page.
notes.evidence: readOnlyRootFilesystem: Mounts the container's root filesystem as read-only.
notes.source: Kubernetes docs, Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container

notes.front: According to NIST SP 800-190, what does running containers with read-only root filesystems achieve?
notes.back: Writes are isolated to specifically defined directories that are easier to monitor, and any tampering is confined there.
notes.explanation: NIST adds that this makes containers more resilient to compromise.
notes.evidence: This approach isolates writes to specifically defined directories, which can then be more easily monitored by the aforementioned tools. Furthermore, using read-only filesystems makes the containers more resilient to compromise since any tampering is isolated to these specific locations
notes.source: NIST SP 800-190, §4.4.4 App vulnerabilities, p. 25

notes.front: Your runtime monitoring struggles because containers write files all over their filesystems. Following NIST SP 800-190, which change confines writes to places that are easy to watch?
choices: Run containers with read-only root filesystems, allowing writes only to specific directories
Run containers as privileged so monitoring agents see more
Turn off runtime monitoring for write events
notes.back: Run containers with read-only root filesystems, allowing writes only to specific directories.
notes.explanation: NIST says read-only roots isolate writes to specifically defined directories, which can then be more easily monitored.
notes.evidence: Containers should also be run with their root filesystems in read-only mode. This approach isolates writes to specifically defined directories, which can then be more easily monitored by the aforementioned tools.

choicesExplained.Give containers larger root filesystems: More space does not limit where writes happen.
choicesExplained.Run containers as privileged so monitori: Privilege widens what the container can do; it does not confine writes.
choicesExplained.Turn off runtime monitoring for write ev: That hides the problem instead of confining the writes.

notes.source: NIST SP 800-190, §4.4.4 App vulnerabilities, p. 25

notes.front: After setting readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, an app crashes because it must write temporary files to /tmp. What keeps the root read-only and lets the app run?
choices: Mount a hostPath volume of the node's /tmp
notes.back: Mount an emptyDir volume at /tmp.
notes.explanation: An emptyDir is a writable scratch space for the Pod, so writes go to one defined directory while the root stays read-only.
notes.evidence: Some uses for an emptyDir are: - scratch space, such as for a disk-based merge sort

choicesExplained.Set readOnlyRootFilesystem: false: That gives up the read-only root the task requires.
choicesExplained.Set privileged: true: Privilege does not make a read-only root writable and weakens isolation.
choicesExplained.Mount a hostPath volume of the node's /t: It exposes the node's filesystem to the Pod, a risk the scratch space does not need.

notes.source: Kubernetes docs, Volumes, “emptyDir”

notes.front: What happens to data in an emptyDir when a container crashes, and when the Pod is removed from its node?
notes.back: A container crash keeps it; removing the Pod from the node deletes it permanently.
notes.explanation: A container crash does not remove the Pod from the node, so the volume survives.
notes.evidence: When a Pod is removed from a node for any reason, the data in the emptyDir is deleted permanently. Note: A container crashing does not remove a Pod from a node. The data in an emptyDir volume is safe across container crashes.
notes.source: Kubernetes docs, Volumes, “emptyDir”

notes.front: What does setting emptyDir.medium to "Memory" do, and what is the catch?
notes.back: Kubernetes mounts a memory-backed tmpfs; files written there count against the writing container's memory limit.
notes.explanation: By default emptyDir uses whatever storage backs the node, such as disk.
notes.evidence: If you set the emptyDir.medium field to "Memory" , Kubernetes mounts a tmpfs (RAM-backed filesystem) for you instead. While tmpfs is very fast, be aware that, unlike disks, files you write count against the memory limit of the container that wrote them.
notes.source: Kubernetes docs, Volumes, “emptyDir”

notes.front: If allowPrivilegeEscalation is not set in a container's securityContext, what is its value?
notes.back: true
notes.explanation: So an immutable, locked-down container has to set allowPrivilegeEscalation: false explicitly.
notes.evidence: If allowPrivilegeEscalation is not defined in the securityContext field of a container specification, then it will default to true.
notes.source: Kubernetes docs, Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container

notes.front: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false cannot be combined with which two container settings?
notes.back: Running as privileged, or having the CAP_SYS_ADMIN capability.
notes.explanation: The docs call the combination inconsistent, so it cannot be set.
notes.evidence: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false is inconsistent, and therefore cannot be set in combination, with a container that: is run as privileged, or has the capability CAP_SYS_ADMIN
notes.source: Kubernetes docs, Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container

notes.front: You must delete every Pod that is not immutable. Which container securityContext passes the check (not privileged, no privilege escalation, read-only root)?
choices: privileged: false, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
notes.back: privileged: false, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
notes.explanation: Only this one sets all three; an unset allowPrivilegeEscalation defaults to true, and an unset readOnlyRootFilesystem leaves the root writable.
notes.evidence: If allowPrivilegeEscalation is not defined in the securityContext field of a container specification, then it will default to true.

choicesExplained.privileged: false, readOnlyRootFilesyste: allowPrivilegeEscalation is unset, so it defaults to true.
choicesExplained.privileged: true, readOnlyRootFilesystem: A privileged container fails the check.
choicesExplained.privileged: false, allowPrivilegeEscalat: Without readOnlyRootFilesystem: true the root filesystem stays writable.

notes.source: Kubernetes docs, Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container

notes.front: On a node, which crictl commands list Pods by name and by label?
notes.back: crictl pods --name <pod-name> and crictl pods --label <key>=<value>.
notes.explanation: crictl pods with no filter lists all Pods on the node.
notes.evidence: List pods by label: crictl pods --label run = nginx
notes.source: Kubernetes docs, Debugging Kubernetes nodes with crictl, “Example crictl commands”

notes.front: What is the difference between crictl ps and crictl ps -a?
notes.back: crictl ps lists running containers; crictl ps -a lists all containers, including stopped ones.
notes.explanation: Without `-a`, containers that have exited are hidden, so `-a` is how you find a container that has already stopped.
notes.evidence: List all containers: crictl ps -a
notes.source: Kubernetes docs, Debugging Kubernetes nodes with crictl, “Example crictl commands”
